words.intro: The MP3 was invented in a German institute. So were the airbag, the jet engine and the chip card. Germans invent very well, and then discuss for ten years whether the rest of the world should have it.

grammar[0].fact: German engineers can spend years on what they call *Technikfolgenabschätzung*, an assessment of the consequences of a technology, before anybody builds it. The Bundestag has had its own office for that since 1990. It’s the sort of word you’d expect.

grammar[1].fact: *Wie* or *als* is the error that gives away even native speakers: *größer wie* is heard on every bus in the south. Teachers still circle it in red. The rule is simple: same is *wie*, different is *als*.

document.intro: A real patent certificate from the German Patent Office, complete with a seal and a ribbon in the colours of the flag. It’s all one sentence again, and all it says is: this is yours. The name of the invention is a German classic.
document.fact: *Mehrscheibenisolierglas* is multi-pane insulating glass, and it’s why German windows are so thick. The Patent Office in Munich handles many thousands of applications a year. Albert Einstein, too, began in a patent office, in Bern.

document.tasks[1].items[2].answer: Es wurde wegen seiner Neuheit patentiert.
reading.intro: A research institute. Dr. Rainer’s team has built a robot that’s meant to carry coffee to the staff. It’s demonstrated to the institute’s director. Lena’s brother, Tim, is a student assistant. He’s the only one who has noticed something about the floor.
reading.photos[1].caption: Ein Institut von oben. Von hier sieht niemand, dass der Boden schief ist.
reading.fact: The Fraunhofer Society is Europe’s largest organisation for applied research, and one of its institutes in Erlangen developed the MP3 format. Germans can rarely resist pointing out that the money was then made elsewhere. There’s a whole phrase for it: *in Deutschland erfunden, anderswo verkauft*.
